KEY MESSAGE 1... Dry conditions with above normal temperatures 
persist through the weekend. This will worsen ongoing water 
resource drought conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
Strong high pressure will sit over New England the next few days
before slowly moving off the coast Saturday night. Friday 
afternoon a cold front passes through from the north, lowering 
temperatures slightly Friday night and Saturday, but still 
keeping temperatures above normal through the weekend. No 
precipitation is expected with the frontal passage. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain is likely Sunday night and Monday. Enough 
rain to make a small dent in the drought is likely.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
The north/west (wetter) trend in the models/ensembles continues,
and a soaking rain now is likely for the whole area. That said,
model agreement is still lower than usual for a system of this
strength at this time range. There is uncertainty in the speed,
strength, and path of the low pressure as it moves northeast up
the East Coast. That said, there is enough confidence to
continue to raise rain chances for the whole area. 

This will be a quick-hitting system, with pretty much all the
rain falling within 12 hours. That said, rain totals could be
pretty impressive along and north/west of the low pressure
center track. The low could track through central Maine, through
the middle of the Gulf of Maine, or anywhere in between. It is
still too early to tell. Rain totals are very uncertain
depending on the low track, but it is likely that somewhere in 
the area will exceed an inch of rain (any spot has about a 70 
percent chance of exceeding an inch). There is even a 30 percent
of any spot exceeding two inches of rain. Keep in mind this is 
all within a 12 hour period, so it will be pretty heavy. While 
flash flooding is unlikely, any leaf-clogged drain could cause 
localized issues. The probabilities for the heavier rain had
been higher for Downeast, but with this continued northward
trend in the models, think that the chances for the heavier
totals are pretty similar throughout the area.

There is no risk of snow with this system, as the airmass will
be quite mild for this time of year. 

Winds along/north of the low pressure track appear pretty light,
but anywhere south of the low track could have some decent south
winds. If the low favors a track on the northern envelope of
solutions, some gusts to around 35 mph are possible along the
coast.

Rain ends by Monday evening, then much colder air rushes in.
Think that there will be enough of a gap between the end of the
rain and temperatures falling below freezing that a widespread
flash freeze of roads is unlikely, though cannot rule out
isolated icy spots Tuesday morning. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...An active weather pattern is likely from 
Thanksgiving into next weekend. Forecast confidence on any 
particular weather system is very low, but travelers should 
continue to monitor this period for potential wintry weather.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
While it is way too far in the future to pinpoint any 
particular weather system, it is important to note that the 
general weather pattern from Thanksgiving through the weekend 
after Thanksgiving is favorable for active weather. This is 
especially important given the active travel period. Looking 
through various ensemble model solutions, timing and system
strength are all over the place. That said, the pattern will be
favorable for Noreasters. About two thirds of ensemble 
solutions have a plowable snow (at least two inches) somewhere 
in Northern/Eastern Maine at some point from Thanksgiving 
through Sunday. We do not want people to be alarmed or alter and
travel plans yet, but rather to be aware of the potential and
continue to check back with us for updates.
